query: Eutectic high-entropy alloys contain dual-phase lamellar colonies with numerous internal boundaries, where microcracking can initiate and lead to catastrophic damage during room-temperature tensile deformation. Conventional processing commonly raises strength at the expense of ductility, while the wide range of previously proposed microstructural-design and processing strategies has not eliminated room-temperature brittleness and limited tensile ductility. Under these constraints, what single intervention could improve both strength and room-temperature tensile ductility? State one testable hypothesis that identifies the intervention, explains its mechanism, predicts outcomes relative to the unmodified lamellar-colony baseline, defines its boundary conditions, cites supporting prior evidence, and proposes an experiment whose result would falsify the hypothesis.

generation.hypothesis: A tailored post‐casting thermal–mechanical treatment that promotes stepwise controllable coherent nanoprecipitations (SCCPs) along the lamellar colony boundaries of eutectic high‐entropy alloys will improve both tensile strength and room‐temperature ductility relative to the conventional as‐cast dual-phase microstructure.
generation.material_initial_state: As-cast eutectic high-entropy alloy with dual-phase lamellar colonies exhibiting numerous internal boundaries that serve as sites for microcrack initiation and cause limited tensile ductility.
generation.intervention: Introduce a controlled annealing/aging process designed to induce coherent nanoprecipitate formation (SCCPs) within the lamellae and along their interfaces.
generation.conditions: A post-casting thermal treatment at an optimized temperature range and cooling rate that enables the formation of uniformly distributed, nanoscale, coherent precipitates without coarsening; mechanical pre-deformation may also be applied immediately prior to aging to promote nucleation.
generation.structural_mediator: The formation of coherent nanoprecipitates that modify the continuity of the brittle phase at the internal boundaries and provide a tailored barrier to dislocation pile-up.
generation.mechanism: Coherent nanoprecipitates are expected to facilitate dislocation transmission and relieve localized stress concentrations at the lamellar boundaries, thereby reducing microcrack initiation while concurrently acting as effective obstacles to dislocation motion, which increases yield strength.
generation.predicted_outcome: Compared to the unmodified lamellar-colony baseline, the treated alloy should exhibit both increased yield strength and enhanced tensile ductility, evidenced by a combination of higher ultimate tensile strength and greater elongation at failure.
generation.baseline: Eutectic high-entropy alloy with a fine, as-cast fcc/B2 lamellar microstructure that suffers from brittle interphase boundaries leading to premature microcracking under tensile loading.
generation.boundary: This intervention is expected to be effective only when the precipitates remain nanoscale and coherent; overaging or conditions that result in incoherent or overly coarse precipitates would likely not yield the improved mechanical properties.
generation.uncertainty: The optimal processing parameters (temperature, time, cooling rate) for inducing SCCPs in eutectic HEAs are not fully determined, and the quantitative degree of strength and ductility improvements remains to be characterized.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare two groups of eutectic HEA samples from the same ingot. Group A (control) will follow the standard as-cast processing route, while group B will undergo the proposed thermal–mechanical treatment designed for SCCP induction. Use transmission electron microscopy (TEM) to examine the presence, distribution, and coherency of nanoprecipitates. Conduct room-temperature tensile tests to compare yield strength, ultimate tensile strength, and elongation.
measurements: TEM imaging for nanoprecipitate size, distribution, and interfacial coherency
Tensile testing to measure yield strength, ultimate tensile strength, and ductility
Fractography to assess microcrack initiation sites and propagation paths
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If group B does not show statistically significant improvements in both tensile strength and room-temperature ductility over the control group, or if TEM reveals that no coherent nanoprecipitates are formed at the critical internal boundaries, then the hypothesis is falsified.

cited_evidence.text: Abstract High-performance refractory alloys with ultrahigh strength and ductility are in demand for a wide range of critical applications, such as plasma-facing components. However, it remains challenging to increase the strength of these alloys without seriously compromising their tensile ductility. Here, we put forward a strategy to “defeat” this trade-off in tungsten refractory high-entropy alloys by stepwise controllable coherent nanoprecipitations (SCCPs). The coherent interfaces of SCCPs facilitate the dislocation transmission and relieve the stress concentrations that can lead to premature crack initiation. As a consequence, our alloy displays an ultrahigh strength of 2.15 GPa with a tensile ductility of 15% at ambient temperature, with a high yield strength of 1.05 GPa at 800 °C. The SCCPs design concept may afford a means to develop a wide range of ultrahigh-strength metallic materials by providing a pathway for alloy design. Subject terms: Metals and alloys, Mechanical engineering
